summary_html: Court orders a **service plan or supervision** period following a substantiated finding. The goal is rehabilitation and reunification consistent with federal 'reasonable-efforts' requirements.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — reasonable-efforts and permanency mandates  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reimbursement framework for foster-care and service costs

primary_citations.citation_text: New York - N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 411 et seq. (Child Protective Services Act – reporting requirements)
New York - Family Court Act Article 10 (Abuse/Neglect juvenile proceedings)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Affirming findings of abuse and an order of supervision, the Court held that Family Court Act § 1046(a)(ii) creates only a rebuttable presumption shifting the burden of going forward to the respondents, while the burden of proving abuse by a preponderance always remains with the petitioning agency.
key_cases.relevance: The disposition was a twelve-month order of supervision with counseling, illustrating court-ordered services short of removal.
key_cases.quote: The establishment of a prima facie case does not require the court to find that the parents were culpable; it merely establishes a rebuttable presumption of parental culpability

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed termination of parental rights for permanent neglect, holding that the agency must first prove diligent efforts and that the parent failed to maintain contact with or plan for the child for more than a year, and that at the separate dispositional hearing the child's best interests control with no presumption favoring return to the parent.
key_cases.relevance: The opinion enumerates the statutory service obligations - counseling, visitation, assistance with housing and employment - that a court-ordered plan must contain.
key_cases.quote: the threshold inquiry by the court in any neglect proceeding must be whether the agency exercised diligent efforts to strengthen the parental relationship

key_cases.holding: The Court held that an agency seeking termination for permanent neglect must affirmatively plead in detail and prove by clear and convincing evidence that it exercised diligent efforts to strengthen the parent-child relationship, and that failure to carry that threshold burden requires dismissal of the petition as to that parent.
key_cases.relevance: It converts the statutory diligent-efforts guidelines into an enforceable, case-specific service obligation on the agency.
key_cases.quote: It has declared as a matter of public policy that the State may not intervene to terminate a parent's rights when assistance in strengthening the family has not been forthcoming

key_cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, First Department
key_cases.holding: The First Department held that Family Court may grant a suspended judgment retroactively after a parent has completed the terms of a dispositional order, vacating the neglect finding and dismissing the petition where that serves the children's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: Full compliance with a court-ordered service plan can be given retroactive effect to erase the underlying finding.
key_cases.quote: Family Court Act § 1051 (c) authorizes dismissal upon two separate and distinct grounds

key_cases.holding: The Court held that Family Court Act article 10-A confers no independent grant of continuing jurisdiction, so once an article 10 neglect petition is dismissed for failure to prove neglect the court loses subject matter jurisdiction and may not conduct further permanency hearings.
key_cases.relevance: Court-ordered supervision and services cannot survive dismissal of the petition that authorized them.
key_cases.quote: the dismissal of a neglect petition terminates Family Court's jurisdiction

key_cases.case_name: Matter of Nassau County Dep't of Social Servs. ex rel. Dante M. v. Denise J.
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a newborn's positive toxicology for a controlled substance cannot by itself support a neglect finding because it does not establish the causative connection to actual or imminent impairment that Family Court Act § 1012(f)(i)(B) requires, but affirmed the findings and the one-year order of supervision because other evidence - prematurity, low birth weight, intensive-care and high-risk follow-up needs, and the mother's cocaine use during pregnancy - showed imminent danger of impairment to both children.
key_cases.relevance: The Court approved a one-year order of supervision as the appropriate level of State intervention where the proof showed risk but no basis for removal.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that more than a positive toxicology is generally required for a neglect determination.
